newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIA METALS - Mining a victim of bureaucracy.
newsitem.headline: INDIA METALS - Mining a victim of bureaucracy.

text.p: Bureaucratic bottlenecks and red tape are hindering India's ambitious plans to capitalise on the investment opportunities offered by its huge mining sector, industry officials and experts said on Tuesday.

They said while there had been an encouraging response to India's decision to allow foreign participation in exploration and mining for high value and scarce minerals as part of structural reforms, the process had several flaws.

"The policy in theory looks all right, the response of foreign and domestic companies is encouraging but the ground realities cannot be ignored," said R.K. Sharma, secretary general of the Federation of Indian Mineral Industries (FIMI), which has 350 mining and metal firms as members.

Last week South Africa's De Beers decided against bidding for diamond mining rights in the central state of Madhya Pradesh after the government refused to let it sell diamonds mined in the state through its Central Selling Organisation (CSO).
The government wanted to sell the diamonds by open auction.

India in 1993 dispensed with the exclusive role of the state sector in exploration and exploitation of 13 minerals including iron ore, manganese ore, gold, diamond, copper, lead, zinc and nickel and threw the doors open to the private sector.
It has made changes in its laws since then to encourage foreign equity investment in the mining sector.

Many Australian, British and Canadian mining firms have expressed interest in the prospecting of gold, diamonds, zinc, copper and lead in the states of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka.
India has rich bauxite, copper, iron ore, lead and granite resources. It is the largest consumer of gold and the biggest centre in the world for diamond cutting and polishing.
Sharma said companies interested in entering India include BHP Minerals (India) Ltd, a unit of Australia's BHP, Pasminco, and CRA Exploration India Ltd, a unit of Rio Tinto Plc/Ltd.
In October 1996 the government responded to investor concerns by increasing the area for prospecting for minerals to 5,000 sq km from 25 sq km per exploration to facilitate aerial prospecting.
Mines Secretary B.B. Tandon told a seminar in London in early July that nine proposals for prospecting over large areas had since been approved.
Mines Minister Birendra Prasad Baishya told reporters in the Indian capital on Tuesday that prospecting licences had been granted over more than 20,000 sq km area.
The companies given approval for prospecting include BHP Mineral India Ltd, CRA Explorationb India Ltd and state-run Hindustan Zinc Ltd.
Baishya said 36 proposals with an investment of 25 billion rupees have been approved for foreign equity participation in mining and allied sectors.
"We have set all the policy parameters in place and things should move," Tandon told the same news conference.
But industry officials and experts said more was needed to quicken the pace.
"In October they increased the area, nine months have lapsed and nothing has happened," said Sharma.
Industry officials said while the government had increased the prospecting area, clearances from the military and civil aviation authorities were needed for aerial prospecting.
"The first hurdle was aerial survey. Now you need to go from door to door," said R. Thakore, FIMI President and director of Calcutta-based Aryan Mining.
Thakore said the government needed to decide if a prospective area was worth exploiting for its minerals or better left untouched as forest reserves.
